A three-item alcohol consumption questionnaire was completed for 61 percent of admissions, usually within three days, and 34 percent of those screened were positive for hazardous or harmful drinking. Only 22 percent of screen-positive patients had any documented alcohol intervention before discharge, and 9 percent were referred to specialist alcohol services. Screening was least often completed for patients admitted under detention and for those discharged within five days. Routine screening identifies many patients with alcohol problems, but in these wards identification rarely led to help."},{"title":"Nurse-delivered brief motivational intervention for harmful drinking among psychiatric inpatients: a single-ward before-after feasibility study","authors":"Quinlan-Adeyemi R, Marsh-Takahashi E, Oduya-Pellegrini S","year":2022,"venue":"Cindervale Mental Health Nursing Review","doi":"10.5555/cmhnr.2022.0314","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We tested whether ward nurses could deliver a two-session brief motivational intervention to inpatients who screened positive for harmful drinking on one acute psychiatric ward. Over eight months, 52 patients screened positive and 41 agreed to take part. Nurses delivered both sessions before discharge to 38 of 52 patients who screened positive, and session recordings showed that 81 percent of core intervention components were delivered. Sessions were most often missed when patients were discharged at short notice. At three months, 24 of 41 participants were reached by telephone. No adverse events related to the intervention were recorded. Delivery by ward nurses appears possible; follow-up was the main difficulty."},{"title":"Brief alcohol interventions for people with severe mental illness: a systematic review of trials","authors":"Petrov-Mensah A, Gallagher-Osei L, Ibrahim-Sandoval K, Whitlock-Obi D","year":2021,"venue":"Vellmar Addiction and Psychiatry Reports","doi":"10.5555/vapr.2021.0077","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We searched five databases for trials of brief alcohol interventions in adults with severe mental illness. Fourteen trials met the inclusion criteria; only two recruited psychiatric inpatients, and both were small. Across trials, effects on drinking at six to twelve months were small and inconsistent, and most trials relied on self-reported drinking with high loss to follow-up. No trial reported harm from the intervention. Trials rarely described who delivered the intervention or how fidelity was checked. The evidence does not show whether brief interventions reduce drinking in this population, and inpatient delivery remains largely untested."},{"title":"Reaching people by telephone three months after psychiatric discharge: response rates and data quality","authors":"Doyle-Karimi F, Andersen-Mbatha T","year":2016,"venue":"Orrinford Journal of Inpatient Psychiatry","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We attempted structured telephone follow-up at three months for 214 adults discharged from two acute psychiatric wards who had agreed to be contacted. Telephone follow-up at three months after psychiatric discharge reached 46 percent of participants, after up to five call attempts. People who were homeless at discharge or had changed their phone number were least often reached. Among those reached, self-reported alcohol use agreed moderately with information in community records. Offering a text message before the call and collecting a second contact number at discharge increased the response rate in the last four months of the study."},{"title":"Acceptability of discussing alcohol during acute psychiatric admission: accounts from patients and nurses","authors":"Kowalczyk-Adebayo J, Fernandez-Lund C","year":2023,"venue":"Cindervale Mental Health Nursing Review","doi":"10.5555/cmhnr.2023.0102","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We held semi-structured conversations with 18 inpatients and 12 nurses on two acute psychiatric wards about discussing alcohol during admission. Patients described being asked about alcohol during admission as acceptable when the question came from their named nurse after the acute crisis had settled. Several patients said that questions asked on the day of admission felt like an accusation. Nurses worried about damaging the therapeutic relationship and about having no time to follow up what patients disclosed. Both groups preferred a short conversation linked to a plan for after discharge. Participants were recruited by ward staff, which may have favoured positive accounts."},{"title":"Progression criteria in feasibility studies of ward-based interventions: a methodological review","authors":"Nakamura-Holt S, Osei-Brandt W, Vasquez-Lind R","year":2024,"venue":"Harthill Trials Methodology Letters","doi":"10.5555/html.2024.0219","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We reviewed 58 published feasibility studies of interventions delivered on hospital wards to see whether they stated criteria for progressing to a larger evaluation. Only 21 of 58 feasibility studies stated progression criteria in advance, and 9 of those used a traffic-light system with green, amber and red thresholds. Studies without pre-stated criteria were more likely to describe their findings as promising whatever their recruitment and retention. Few studies reported confidence intervals for feasibility estimates. We recommend stating progression criteria before recruitment, with thresholds for recruitment, delivery and follow-up, and reporting feasibility estimates with their precision."},{"title":"Fidelity of nurse-delivered brief interventions during busy shifts: an observational study on medical and psychiatric wards","authors":"Brennan-Achterberg L, Silva-Nakashima H","year":2018,"venue":"Harthill Trials Methodology Letters","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We observed 96 brief intervention sessions delivered by nurses on medical and psychiatric wards and rated fidelity against a checklist of core components. Mean fidelity was 72 percent on medical wards and 64 percent on psychiatric wards. Fidelity fell when the nurse was also responsible for more than six patients and when the session was interrupted. Sessions delivered in a quiet room scored higher than bedside sessions. Nurses said a pocket card with the core steps helped them keep sessions short and complete. The observer was present in every session, which may have raised fidelity."}]}
